clue.text: To be a luvvie and drink is a pain in the arse

definitions.text: is a pain in the arse

parts.note: a luvvie is a theatrical type, and what one does is act; the clue's 'is' supplies the S
sup means drink, read here as S plus UP split across the join

explanation.surface: A theatrical type who also drinks heavily is an irritating person to be around.
explanation.walkthrough: Really ACT plus SUP: to act is what a luvvie does, and sup is to drink. A luvvie is British slang for a gushing, self-regarding actor.
explanation.definitionFit: To behave badly and make trouble is exactly what makes someone an irritating nuisance, so the idiom matches the verb phrase.

clue.text: "Dead end" suitably clued as "Leader of Conservatives"

parts.note: surface reading: a road closed at one end, offered as a clue
setter's reading: a jibe that the Tory leader leads his party nowhere; the French word for a backside lurks in it too

explanation.walkthrough: A satirical jab: the same phrase that defines a dead-end street is offered as a fitting description of the Conservative leader, a political road to nowhere.
explanation.definitionFit: A street with only one way in and out is a blind alley, literally 'bottom of the bag' in French.

clue.text: Seat that's been evacuated

definitions.meaning: second meaning: what the bowels pass, a medical word for faeces

explanation.surface: A chair left behind after everyone has cleared the building.
explanation.walkthrough: Evacuated suggests people leaving a building; here it is the bowels being emptied.
explanation.definitionFit: The word means both a backless seat and a piece of faeces, the medical term for excreted matter.

clue.text: Leaders of protest rubbish old campaigning rock singer for the public good, in short

definitions.text: for the public good, in short

indicators.note: leaders are what go in front, so only the opening letters are kept

parts.note: first letters of protest, rubbish and old
Bono of U2 is famous for campaigning against poverty

explanation.surface: Protest leaders dismiss an ageing activist rock star as a do-gooder.
explanation.walkthrough: 'In short' because the phrase is shortened from the Latin pro bono publico.
explanation.definitionFit: Pro bono publico is Latin for the welfare of the community; the short form now means unpaid charitable work.

clue.text: Drink breaks as announced by piss-artist?

indicators.note: a piss-artist is a drunk, so this is how the word comes out when slurred by one

parts.note: breaks are snaps; a drunk slurs the S into SH

explanation.surface: A pub bore who drinks a lot tells everyone when the drinking intervals are.
explanation.walkthrough: Snaps (breaks) slurred by a drunk becomes 'shnaps'. Piss-artist is British slang for a heavy drinker.
explanation.definitionFit: Schnapps is a strong spirit, so it is a kind of alcoholic beverage, an example of the general word.

clue.text: That accidental admission re. Iraq by Blair? – (i.e. reason for failing to administer a proper licking)

definitions.text: That accidental admission re. Iraq by Blair?
definitions.meaning: first meaning: an unintended remark, as when a politician lets the truth out

definitions.text: reason for failing to administer a proper licking
definitions.meaning: second meaning, taken literally: if the organ you lick with slides off, the lick is botched

explanation.surface: Tony Blair blurted something about Iraq, and in brackets the setter makes a joke about poor licking.
explanation.walkthrough: The bracketed half reads the idiom literally: the organ in your mouth slipping is why a lick goes wrong.
explanation.definitionFit: A verbal blunder where words come out by mistake, revealing what the speaker did not mean to say.

clue.text: Honk rap that's commonplace

parts.note: honk and hum are both British slang for a bad smell
to rap is to drum with the fingers

explanation.surface: A sneer that a car horn and rap music are both boringly ordinary.
explanation.walkthrough: Honk suggests a car horn; in British slang it means to stink, as does hum.
explanation.definitionFit: Humdrum means dull and ordinary, lacking any excitement, so it is a synonym for unremarkable.

clue.text: Awkward, having only members that oppose

definitions.meaning: first meaning: clumsy with the hands
second meaning, literally: every digit on the hand is the opposable kind

explanation.surface: A difficult committee made up entirely of members who vote against everything.
explanation.walkthrough: Members means limbs or digits, not committee members; the thumb is the opposable digit.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone who is all thumbs is clumsy and fumbling, an idiom for lacking dexterity.

clue.text: Rub up Victoria round tops of legs (inside)

indicators.note: round means one word encircles another

parts.note: Victoria Beckham was Posh Spice

indicators.note: the tops of words are their initial letters

parts.note: first letters of legs and inside

explanation.surface: Someone rubs Victoria's upper thighs, in a smutty aside.
explanation.walkthrough: '(inside)' looks like inner thighs, but it is just a word giving its first letter. Posh Spice was Victoria Beckham's name in the Spice Girls.
explanation.definitionFit: To polish is to rub a surface until it shines, so it is the same as buffing something up.

clue.text: Is local corruption and head from Monroe about the crux of John Kennedy's problem?

indicators.note: corruption spoils something's proper form, so these letters are scrambled

parts.note: taken as written

indicators.note: the head of a word is its opening letter, so only that is kept

parts.note: first letter of Monroe

indicators.note: a crux is the heart of something, so the central letters are kept

parts.note: the two middle letters of John

explanation.surface: A conspiracy theory linking local corruption and Marilyn Monroe to President Kennedy's troubles.
explanation.walkthrough: It is not the president: Charles Kennedy, Liberal Democrat leader, resigned in 2006 after admitting a drink problem. 'About' merely joins the pieces.
explanation.definitionFit: Charles Kennedy publicly admitted dependence on drink, so his well-known problem was addiction to alcohol.

clue.text: Way of showing online amusement at Labour's chief slouch

indicators.note: the chief part of a word is its leading letter, which alone is kept

parts.note: first letter of Labour
LOL, 'laughing out loud', the online way of showing amusement, placed after the L

explanation.surface: Someone sniggers online at the lazy posture of the Labour leader.
explanation.walkthrough: The order is L followed by LOL, the text-speak for laughing out loud.
explanation.definitionFit: To loll is to lounge or sprawl lazily, a synonym for slumping in a slack posture.

clue.text: Flapping old towel and rolling in it

indicators.note: something flapping is being tossed about, so its letters fly into a new order

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone flaps an old towel about and rolls around in it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Rolling in it' looks like more of the towel scene, but it is the idiom for being rich.
explanation.definitionFit: Being rolling in it is an idiom for having plenty of money, as prosperous people do.

clue.text: Fashion again is about taking a drug

parts.note: re means about, concerning
hash is short for hashish, a drug

explanation.surface: Restyling something counts as being about drug use.
explanation.definitionFit: To rehash is to rework old material into a new form, which is making it over a second time.

clue.text: & 20 Peter, in shady parlance, needs arse, as preferred by parliamentary candidate

definitions.note: the answer is a noun phrase; the definition describes it as what a candidate prefers

parts.note: peter is criminal slang for a safe
one's seat is one's backside

explanation.surface: A crook talks about a parliamentary candidate who needs a backside to sit on.
explanation.walkthrough: In old criminal slang a peter is a safe, as in peterman, a safecracker.
explanation.definitionFit: A constituency where one party's majority is huge is what any candidate hopes for, guaranteeing election to Parliament.

clue.text: One of many Nixon had to take out?

definitions.text: One of many Nixon had to take out?

parts.words: One of many Nixon had to take out
parts.note: surface reading: something President Nixon had to remove, perhaps an enemy or a date
setter's reading: the published Watergate tape transcripts were full of 'deleted' swear words

explanation.walkthrough: The Watergate tape transcripts famously replaced Nixon's swearing with a bracketed '(deleted)' note, over and over.
explanation.definitionFit: A swear word is the thing censored again and again from Nixon's recorded conversations.

clue.text: The best possible pot, sadly one not forthcoming

indicators.note: sadly suggests something gone wrong, so these letters are knocked out of order

parts.note: pot rearranged
Roman numeral one
mum means silent, saying nothing

explanation.surface: The ideal jackpot, unfortunately, is the one that never materialises.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Keep mum' means stay silent, so mum is someone not forthcoming.
explanation.definitionFit: Optimum means the most favourable or ideal condition, a direct synonym for the finest achievable.

clue.text: Indiscreet, tense? Don't make so much of a performance of it!

parts.note: T is the grammar abbreviation for tense

parts.words: Don't make so much of a performance of it
parts.note: an instruction to act less, to perform less

explanation.surface: Someone tense and blurting things out is told to stop being so dramatic.
explanation.definitionFit: Tactless describes saying things that offend for lack of sensitivity, the same as being careless about secrets.

clue.text: Cheap-to-make radio programme, producing Peg Gobbles Hard One

indicators.note: to gobble is to swallow, so one word ends up inside the other

parts.note: a peg is a pin
H for hard, as on pencils
taken as written

explanation.surface: A budget radio show is described like a headline about a woman named Peg eating something tough.
explanation.definitionFit: A phone-in show fills airtime with listeners' calls, so it costs little to produce.

clue.text: Wrinkly Rod's let out

indicators.note: out means disordered or wrong, so these letters are rearranged

parts.note: taken as written, the apostrophe dropped

explanation.surface: Ageing rocker Rod Stewart has been released.
explanation.walkthrough: Wrinkly is British slang for an old person, a noun here.
explanation.definitionFit: An oldster is an elderly person, the same slang sense of an aged, creased-skinned pensioner.

clue.text: After snog, truss is smart wear

parts.note: to neck is to kiss passionately, as is to snog
to truss is to tie up

explanation.surface: After a kiss, tying someone up counts as stylish dressing.
explanation.walkthrough: Snog is British slang for a long kiss.
explanation.definitionFit: A necktie is worn with a suit for formal occasions, an example of dressy clothing.

clue.text: see 13
Kay twiddled thing for board member

indicators.note: twiddling means turning things about, so the letters get rearranged

parts.note: kay is the spelt-out name of the letter K
thing rearranged

explanation.surface: A woman named Kay fiddles with a gadget to win a seat on the company board.
explanation.walkthrough: Board member suggests a company director; the board here is a chessboard.
explanation.definitionFit: The knight is a piece that moves about a chessboard, so it is one of the board's pieces.

clue.text: Peacekeepers to be joined by Crouch? Relax!

parts.note: the United Nations sends peacekeeping forces
to crouch is to bend down

explanation.surface: UN troops get striker Peter Crouch, then someone tells everyone to calm down.
explanation.walkthrough: Crouch, capitalised, suggests the England footballer Peter Crouch, but it is the plain verb.
explanation.definitionFit: To unbend is to loosen up and become less formal, which is what someone told to calm down does.

clue.text: -Kiss very big copper on behind

parts.note: OS is outsize, a clothing size
Cu is the chemical symbol for copper
behind schedule is late

explanation.surface: An invitation to kiss a very big policeman on his bottom.
explanation.walkthrough: Behind looks like the backside, but it means overdue. Copper is British slang for a police officer.
explanation.definitionFit: To osculate is the formal, almost scientific word for kissing, a learned synonym.

clue.text: Flashy Lulu ridiculed somewhat

indicators.note: somewhat means a part only, so a stretch of the words is used

parts.note: letters running across the two words

explanation.surface: The pop singer Lulu, mocked for her flamboyant style.
explanation.definitionFit: Lurid means gaudy and garishly bright, so it is a synonym for showy.

clue.text: Fruity thing, unattractive, given 'oral' treatment

indicators.note: oral treatment means the word is spoken rather than written

parts.note: unattractive means ugly

explanation.surface: An unappealing piece of fruit is given some sort of oral attention.
explanation.walkthrough: The ugli is a Jamaican citrus fruit, named for its wrinkled look.
explanation.definitionFit: The ugli is a citrus hybrid of grapefruit and tangerine, so it is a fruit.

clue.text: Mean — pissed on poor dears

indicators.note: poor means in bad shape, so these letters are broken up and rebuilt

parts.note: pissed and tight both mean drunk
dears rearranged

explanation.surface: A drunk relieving himself on some unfortunate old ladies is being nasty.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Pissed on' wants to be one action, but pissed is drunk and on just joins.
explanation.definitionFit: Tight-arsed is coarse slang for stingy with money, matching mean in its miserly sense.

clue.text: Patriotic figure shows way to get stuffed outside England's capital

parts.note: St is short for street

indicators.note: outside means one word wraps round the other

parts.note: to gorge is to stuff oneself with food

indicators.note: 'capital' keeps only the first letter of 'England'

parts.note: the capital letter of England

explanation.surface: A flag-waving figure tells someone where to go, rudely, outside London.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Get stuffed' looks like a rude dismissal but means eat a lot. St George is England's patron saint.
explanation.definitionFit: England's patron saint appears on the national flag and is invoked by English patriots.

clue.text: Start of David Steel's downfall? Having no senior

indicators.note: a downfall is a collapse, so the letters tumble into a new order
the start of a word is its opening letter, which alone is kept

parts.note: first letter of David
taken as written, the possessive tying it to the next word

explanation.surface: The beginning of Liberal leader David Steel's fall from power came with no older figure above him.
explanation.walkthrough: David Steel looks like one name, the former Liberal leader, but only his initial joins the surname in the jumble.
explanation.definitionFit: The eldest child is the oldest, so nobody in the family ranks above them by age.
